Is there a way we could we could help with this? for instance:

  • if there's a list of theorems it would be worth cleaning up in mathlib style, we could have Claude do it. e.g. we can definitely complete the parts of Mazur's theorem we didn't need for this proof.
  • we can just ask Claude which results it proved that would be significantly helpful for Mathlib etc.

Some of this this people besides us can probably do, but anything that needs to be more scalable we can try to help with.

This is why I was mentioning tau ceti, you can just tell Claude find the bits that are wanted for the roadmaps there and PR them and also contributing AIs for the reviews. This is something where scaling up would be quite welcome.
In fact I'd be happy to make some more roadmaps to incorporate more bits of the proof, so that would help with the knowing what bits would be useful to cleanup and PR.

In no particular order:

  • Extract errata for published mathematics (it seems someone has done this in the other thread).
  • Extract digestion insights into all that mathematics.
  • Extract insights into what approaches do or do not work well for formalizing these kinds of mathematics.
  • Extract the thousands of small lemmas and other bits of missing API for existing parts of mathlib that must be implicit in any formalization of this size and get them into mathlib (and refactor the formalization as you go along to make use of things added to mathlib).
  • For all the known-in-1980s pieces that are also of use for the modern proof, clean them up to mathlib standards and generality and get them into mathlib, where this doesn't conflict with other ongoing work on those pieces of mathematics, so the modern proof can end up depending only on mathlib. (And again, refactor this formalization to use those pieces as they get into mathlib.)
  • Get from "all of 100-theorems formalized in some ITP" to "all of 100-theorems formalized in mathlib". (I'm guessing we're probably already at "all of 100-theorems formalized in Lean" if you include slop autoformalizations not linked from our website, since the remaining non-FLT ones must be much easier than FLT; again, it's quality and integration that are the remaining interesting parts.)
  • Do the full modularity theorem (but I don't think that's particularly interesting until the AI is ready to do it to mathlib quality and get it into mathlib, since there can't be much doubt that AI could do a messy formalization now).

While I would love to see everything you just said, I'm not sure if the mathlib community wants all of FLT in mathlib (unfortunately), even if one day all the code becomes "mathlib-quality" whatever that means.

Seriously, I expect 98 of the 100 theorems could (and should) go in either mathlib or the mathlib archive (if genuinely leaf results of no real importance or likelihood of being used in anything else) without causing any major technical problems (in terms of build time etc.). I think most of the mathematics in FLT is important enough (and not leaf results) to be worth including in mathlib; it depends on how much cleanup reduces code size and resources required to build it whether it can go in single-repository mathlib or is part of what requires mathlib to split into multiple repositories. (The four colour theorem is the other one where the size of the proof might be an issue with mathlib inclusion.)

If it's possible for us, speaking for myself, I'd like to make this more useful to people.

I encourage this version to be archived. Then an effort (possibly AI-directed) should be made to refactor the code to a smaller and more intelligible version. Most importantly, where possible have the refactoring come with a certificate of correctness, so that the refactored code can be proven to achieve the same important properties of the original version, primarily that it constitutes a machine checkable proof of FLT, and that the new version has "provable" improvements which result in a good reason for the refactor. (THis way, there is another path to show that the proof is correct, this second path being intentionally more robust in the face of changes to Lean and Mathlib.) Eventually, after a series of machine-verfied refactors, the latest version of the FLT proof may become comprehensible to non-AI entities. However, the first step is to archive (and establish multiple copies of the archive) the current artifact: If this artifact is correct (represents a correct formalized proof), future generations will want to verify it, and if it isn't correct, there is historical precedent for keeping it around for study and improvement.

I asked Claude what it thought the most feasible & valuable pieces for Mathlib would be:

Realistically, about a dozen small results could reach Mathlib soon as human rewrites. The big number-theory infrastructure is worth more, but each piece would be a project-scale redo with the Imperial and Mathlib people, not a copy.

→ Top picks, all stated on Mathlib's own objects, with proofs that rest only on Mathlib:

  • Class number one for Q(ζ11)\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{11})Q(ζ11​) and Q(ζ13)\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{13})Q(ζ13​). Same statement as Mathlib's p=3p = 3p=3 and 555, so it's the closest thing to a drop-in PR.
  • Finite-dimensionality and dimension bounds for Mk(Γ)M_k(\Gamma)Mk​(Γ) and Sk(Γ0(N))S_k(\Gamma_0(N))Sk​(Γ0​(N)), plus a Sturm bound. Mathlib has these for level one only.
  • S2(Γ0(2))=0S_2(\Gamma_0(2)) = 0S2​(Γ0​(2))=0, the last step of the proof, in 216 lines.
  • Fermat for exponent 5. Mathlib has exponents 3 and 4.
  • The Wiles–Lenstra numerical criterion, the commutative algebra behind R=TR = \mathbb{T}R=T, in full generality. Worth asking the Imperial project first.

Also the Jacobi triple product, and two literal TODOs in Mathlib's source: Selmer-group finiteness and the S-unit theorem.

→ Most valuable, but project-scale: Hecke operators on classical modular forms, finite flat group schemes with the Fontaine theory at p=3p = 3p=3, modular curves with their Jacobians, and the Tate curve. Mathlib has none of these at our pin, and each would go in as a human-led development with our files as a worked reference.

I see a lot of chatter about Tau Ceti, which could be a natural spot for this to land? I can imagine formal proofs advancing on two fronts: (1) a clean library like Mathlib intended for humans and (2) an AI-driven library backed by something like Prove2Me (or an alternative) that grows as fast as possible under a collaborative blueprint. Completed proofs that pass some automated style/correctness review could be automatically PRed and approved. I don't know if that's what Tau Ceti has in mind, but it would be neat if larger AI-driven projects could be completed collaboratively in the open with low friction.

Jacob Austin said:

Selmer-group finiteness and the S-unit theorem.

Note that this is available in my EllipticCurves repo (I'd venture the guess that it's closer to Mathlib quality there).

I don't think we want the class number calculations. As for modular form results, those are all already outlined in a tau ceti roadmap, same for hecke operators and modular curves, etc. You could just point Claude at that and make PRs. Tau ceti is a AI-driven library with some quality checks (done by AI) so it would benefit from some scaling by more AIs.

I also asked Claude to do a careful read of the proof and the Tau Ceti roadmaps and see what would be easy to add:

What could be contributed now (items that match open roadmap entries):

  • AlgebraicCurves: finiteness of the integral closure for finite-type domains over a field, with no separability assumption. This is an open item there, and we prove it over Mathlib alone. For its later layers: our function-field Riemann–Roch, Riemann–Hurwitz over kˉ\bar kkˉ and residue theorem.
  • JacobianChallenge: a Jacobian over k=kˉk = \bar kk=kˉ, meaning a smooth proper scheme representing rigidified Pic0\mathrm{Pic}^0Pic0, with Abel–Jacobi. That roadmap doesn't have this yet.
  • ModularForms: the dimension formula for S2(Γ0(N))S_2(\Gamma_0(N))S2​(Γ0​(N)) at every level. This is the weight-2 case of what the roadmap calls its hardest target. We prove it algebraically and the roadmap wants the analytic proof, so this starts as a conversation with its author.
  • EllipticCurves and ClassFieldTheory, once their earlier layers exist: E[n]≅(Z/n)2E[n] \cong (\mathbb{Z}/n)^2E[n]≅(Z/n)2 over Kˉ\bar KKˉ for nnn invertible, the Weil pairing, the Tate module TℓET_\ell ETℓ​E with its Galois action, Tate-curve results over ppp-adic fields, and Tate cohomology H^∗\hat H^\astH^∗ (cup products, Herbrand quotients).

Already covered. A few things we'd have offered are already in Tau Ceti or on their way into Mathlib: the Sturm bound and finite-dimensionality of Mk(Γ)M_k(\Gamma)Mk​(Γ), Hecke operators TnT_nTn​, Selmer-group finiteness, and SSS-units.

What has no roadmap yet. This is more than half of the proof:

  • modular curves as algebraic curves, J0(N)J_0(N)J0​(N) and Néron models, Eichler–Shimura and the Eisenstein ideal;
  • the automorphic side (Jacquet–Langlands, base change, Langlands–Tunnell);
  • deformation theory and R=TR = \mathbb{T}R=T;
  • finite flat group schemes;
  • the main Frey–Ribet–Mazur–Wiles argument.

Each would first need a roadmap written and owned by a person. Finite flat group schemes looks like the easiest to propose, because it connects to things Tau Ceti already has.

Many of the bigger intermediate theorems (Mazur, Ribet, Langlands-Tunnell) weren't proven in full for FLT, although these could be completed. They're also not on Tau Ceti's roadmap.

Anyway, the rough TLDR seems to be that we could land quite a lot in Tau Ceti if those would be welcome, but also much of the proof is absent from any roadmap as far as I can tell.

Yeah so there is a draft roadmap on modular curves that could take lots of the modular curve stuff and we can make more roadmaps for the other reusable bits to get in, but starting with that list above would be great!
@Chris Birkbeck would your skill be relevant here https://github.com/CBirkbeck/mathlib-quality

Not directly at this scale. For something like this I think one needs to essentially start from the ground up and take little pieces and cleanup each one (at that point you could use something like my skill). At this scale, just trying to clean it up would be a bigger job than producing the proof.

I can imagine formal proofs advancing on two fronts: (1) a clean library like Mathlib intended for humans and (2) an AI-driven library backed by something like Prove2Me (or an alternative) that grows as fast as possible under a collaborative blueprint. As we generate many proofs, maybe there is a way to judge which “paths” to the proof are cleaner or more palatable for humans before canonicalizing them into mathlib. I’d be happy to explore building a system like this on prove2me.
